sections.html: Chindongo socolofi is one of the smallest mbuna. In the wild they barely exceed 8 cm in length; in the aquarium they can grow 50% larger. The species is relatively peaceful in the aquarium.

The colours of the mbuna serve to demarcate species from one another as clearly as possible. This makes it easier to recognise one's own species and avoids fights, since members of other species usually eat something else and there is less need to fight over food and females. Among the most combative mbuna is C. bellicosus, the type species of the genus. Chindongo socolofi, however, is relatively peaceful in the aquarium.

In many mbuna there is clear gender dichromatism: sexually mature males are coloured differently than females, and juveniles all look like females. Only sexually mature males defend territories and signal with showy colours that they invite passing females to mate; other males in showy colours are beaten up.
In Chindongo socolofi males and females cannot be distinguished by colour. Only the egg spots in the anal fin are missing in the females or are at least less pronounced.

The genus Chindongo was described in 2016 together with its type species C. bellicosus. It includes C. ater, C. bellicosus, C. cyaneus, C. demasoni, C. elongatus, C. flavus, C. heteropictus, C. longior, C. minutus, C. saulosi and C. socolofi.
